1.	All the formations of the Canadian forces serving in the Far East form part of the United Nations forces under the command of the supreme commander. subtopic: EASTER ADJOURNMENT

speechtext:
Righl Hon. L. S. Si. Laurenl (Prime Minister) moved:
That when this house adjourns at 10 o'clock p.m. on Thursday, April 2nd next, it stand adjourned until Tuesday, April 7th next, at 2.30 o'clock p.m.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I had the advantage of discussing with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leaders of the other groups, on Thursday, the kind of motion it would be proper to make for the Easter adjournment. I think all four of us were under the impression that it was still the hope of hon. members that it might be possible to finish the work of the session, without undue haste or without neglecting anything that should be done in connection with it, by the end of April or the beginning of May.
In order to make that possible, we felt it would be desirable to have as short an adjournment at Easter as could reasonably be contemplated. There seemed to be no alternative to either having the adjournment from Thursday night to Tuesday morning or having it for at least ten days so that hon. members who reside at considerable distances from Ottawa would have time to go home and get back. It was felt that if that were not going to be possible it would be rather unfair to them to keep them in Ottawa without sittings of the house any longer than was absolutely necessary.
As a result of that conference I agreed to put down this motion for the adjournment from Thursday night until Tuesday afternoon to cover only the two holidays of Good Friday and Easter Monday. I am sure that no hon. member would feel it was proper to be sitting on Good Friday, and having to take the longer week end I think it is also desirable not to sit on Easter Monday, which most other Canadians will be taking as a holiday as well.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to continue to discuss certain reasons why I believe that assurance should be given to the hon. members of this house that steps will be taken to review the whole organization of government and the administration of its departments even though we recognize that it would not be possible for such inquiry to be conducted and completed before the budget has been dealt with or the estimates of the departments presented to the members of this house.
Events of the past few days which have occupied so much time over the radio and in the press do remind us that we are in a twilight period of half war and half peace. The unity of the free world gives us hope that peace may in fact be assured for all of us, but that does not dispose of the fact that there is at this very moment a very real war in Korea and that there is fighting elsewhere throughout the world. What has been happening in these past few days, increasing tension between the free world and the slave world, warns us that we are living through something that is little more than an uneasy armistice, with peace still to
2962	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew be assured only by the efforts of the free peoples who are combining to make sure that the elements of danger do not get beyond control.
We are told that the Korean war has cost us $129 million, but we should remember, and particularly at this time, that in the same period the people of this country have been called upon to spend for defence some $4,000 million. Every Canadian, every person loyal to democratic government, either in Canada or elsewhere, hopes for peace above all else. However, there is no escaping the fact that these enormous expenditures, part of which we have presented to us now, are made in the hope of avoiding a general war but also have been made and are being made with the recognition that we might actually become engaged in a war unless the effectiveness of our effort were maintained.
If the preparations for defence on the limited basis which has already been undertaken is to cost us so much money for that part which is not represented by fighting itself, then surely it does not take very much imagination to realize what would happen in the unhappy and terrible event that we actually did become engaged in another war.
Surely it is not necessary to press this argument. One of the factors which the men in the Kremlin surely must be keeping in their minds at all times is the ability of the free nations to maintain their military effort in the event that war did break out. If they became convinced that the free nations were going to impose too great a strain on their economy by the efforts which would require to be undertaken to defend freedom, then that would be as important a factor in their consideration as the number of tanks, aircraft and other pieces of military equipment which are regarded so carefully by all nations at this time.
Our survival in war as well as the survival of our free economy in peace demands that every possible step be taken now which will make our expenditure of money and effort as efficient as possible. If the government were only prepared to say to the members of this house, and through the members of this house to the people of Canada, that they are disturbed by what they have learned, and are ready to deal with the waste and extravagance which has been brought to their attention, then hon. members of this house might have some feeling of reassurance that in spite of all that has been exposed some steps are going to be taken to bring this to an end.
Instead of any such reassuring statement, however, the government says in simple and 

unequivocal terms that there is no foundation for the suggestion that waste, extravagance and inefficiency exist.
There is one very serious consequence of this and one which perhaps is not sufficiently brought to the attention of members of this house in the discussions which take place from time to time. Every government official in every department of government knows perfectly well that there is waste and extravagance. Every government official sees waste and extravagance just as those Canadians who are in places where it can be seen also see waste and extravagance. If those government officials come to the conclusion that what they now see is not to be regarded as waste and extravagance by the government, then surely there can be little encouragement to them To tackle those examples that come to their attention. We know that there is no single thing which will so seriously hold up or increase inflation as will extravagance and waste which offer no productive result. The answer to inflation is efficient production, and efficient production will largely be affected by the extent to which efficiency is to be found at or near the top.
It is true that inflation has been checked. We will hope that this is not temporary. Of course there is one question that arises in our minds. We see one of those things which require further explanation in a recent report. We find that the new price index suggests a slight reduction in the cost of living whereas the cost of living index to which so many of our wage contracts in this country have been anchored shows an increase at the same time. Whichever is correct, however, the fact remains that inflation may be regarded as standing still for the present. That fact, however, is no reason for complacency. What we should be doing is to take every step that can be taken not only to halt the increase in inflation but also to reduce inflation by the assurance that every effective economy has been undertaken.
When the suggestion is made that something should be done to examine this situation in the way that every business is bound to examine its own affairs from time to time, we are told that in this suggestion we should be more specific. After all, Mr. Speaker, this again is one of the disturbing things about the situation before us. We have the report of the Auditor General disclosing the fact that there are eight different systems of accounting and that nothing effective is being done to unify them. Is that not specific enough for this government? There is no indication that it is.

The government asks us to be specific in other respects. We have the findings of a man described on different occasions by the government as the man best qualified in Canada to undertake the inquiry that he undertook. We have his extremely explicit findings of waste, extravagance, inefficiency and theft. Moreover, he found that there had been a complete breakdown in the administrative supervision of the department which is spending half of our tax money and that there has been widespread inefficiency. Is that not specific enough for the government?
We have had read to us passages from the Gordon report which we have not seen and cannot obtain. It apparently makes the most explicit findings with regard to inefficiency. Mr. Speaker, there were read into the record of this house on March 12, by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), words purporting to be from what is known as the Gordon report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) raises an extremely interesting point. It will be recalled that only a few days ago, in response to a request for the production of reports, a minister of the government explained that it would not be possible to produce those reports because of the amount of time and effort that would be devoted to obtaining them. Either that statement was correct or it was not. If that statement was correct, then I must confess that I find it difficult to know how the Prime Minister is in a position to say that he can say positively that no words of this kind appear in any of these reports. Either the government has the reports or it has not. If the government has a collection of reports sufficiently comprehensive for the Prime Minister to say, "Those words do not appear" or "Words to this effect do not appear", or if the government has had made a digest of the reports which makes it possible for any member of this government to say "These words do not appear in any reports we have", then the answer that these reports are not available was not an answer in accordance with the facts. It is one thing or the other. Either these reports are available and they should be made available to the members of this house, or they are not available. If they are not available, then time should be devoted to getting them. This situation is such that one of the things which the government should have undertaken long ago was to get together all the reports that had been made with regard to the different activities of this government, in view of what was found in the case where we have had at least an extremely limited view of the administration and supervision of government activities.
I leave the matter there. If the reports are available in such a way that the Prime Minister feels confident with regard to what they contain, may I simply ask the Prime Minister whether he will now undertake to
2964	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew present and to table in this house the reports to which he refers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I will not. It has never been the practice to do so. We are operating under a constitutional system whereby it is the ministers who are responsible for the decisions that are made. It has always been the recognized practice for it to be the privilege of ministers to get confidential reports from those in whom they may have confidence. But those reports have always been treated as confidential reports. It would be drying up the source from which ministers responsible to this house can get assistance if it became known that they could not get any assistance in a confidential way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is indeed a
declaration of a new concept of parliamentary responsibility. The government is merely the executive of this parliament, and is merely the executive body responsible for administration. Any money that is spent on obtaining reports for the purpose of examining the details of any department is taxpayers' money. The reports are the property of the taxpayers, and we as the representatives of the taxpayers have the right to see those reports unless they are properly subject to some terms of secrecy, such as would be involved in the case of secret documents relating to national defence. There can be no other case where this government, or any other government, has the right to refuse to the members of this house reports which were made for the purpose of examining the administration of the departments and suggesting improvements in the business of government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

I quite agree with the
Leader of the Opposition that the government cannot refuse to a majority of parliament anything that the majority of parliament requests, but the majority in parliament, so long as it has confidence in the government, has not required the government to disclose the information it obtains in a confidential manner.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Minorities must rule.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is a denial of the one
basis upon which our parliamentary system operates. Our parliamentary system operates on the basis that the minority has the right to access to information which would make it possible to form a proper opinion about anything coming before the house. The


principle just enunciated by the Prime Minister would apply with equal force to any other document that ordinarily would be tabled in this house, and make production subject to a majority vote, which has a habit of following the express desire of the government in that respect. Then, it would be possible for this government completely to change the established procedure that has been accepted by this house as the basis of our parliamentary procedure ever since 1867.
At least, Mr. Speaker, we have this much before us now. We know now that there was not very much in the contention that it was because of the amount of work it would have taken to get the reports that we did not get them. We know now that it is simply because the Prime Minister asserts that the government has the right to say what we shall be able to see and what we shall not. If that is the proposition, let us know it. Let not any of us be misled into the belief that the reason was that it was going to take too long to find out where the reports were, or what reports could be presented. This proposition is a simple one. The proposition now put forward by the government is simply this. You will just get as much information as we are prepared to give you, and as long as we are able to get the majority vote of our members, that is going to be just as little as you can possibly get. That is the situation, and that now explains why the committees of this house have been so ineffective in being able to get the kind of information that we had hoped they would be able to get when they were originally set up.
The majority rules, yes; but the old idea of majority rule was that it would be with full knowledge that is now to be denied. It is just to be such measure of knowledge as the majority in its discretion thinks at any time the opposition is entitled to have. That is the proposition which is apparently now to remain part of our parliamentary practice here for such time as this government holds office.
This government has only emphasized why we should continue to seek by every device we can information in regard to other aspects of government administration. I used the comparison before, but in view of the proposition now before us I repeat that comparison. When we are told that we shall see just so much as the government decides we can see, then it is necessary for us to remember that we have before us what in effect constitutes a large administrative structure with one hundred rooms. We got a peep through the window of one room, because the government in that case did

decide that we would be permitted to see the Currie report. Perhaps the only reason we saw that was that it had seen the light of day in some other way. But in any event, we did see into that room. We saw into one room and we saw a disgracefully untidy room.
The government asks us to be specific. Well, what we saw there was clear and definite enough. We saw there the records of the stolen siding, of the lost bags of cement, of the pleasant fishpond and of the horses on the payroll, and the other things that were disclosed in that room. But we have not seen through any one of the other ninety-nine windows. Now we are told that it is not likely that we are going to get a peek through any of the other ninety-nine windows. Of course the fact remains that we have had some opportunity at least to get an idea of what some of these rooms do contain.
We have asked the government to let the other blinds go up, and to let us see what is in those other rooms so that if necessary there can be a housecleaning. After all, this administrative structure belongs to the people of Canada, not to this government. The government is not even the tenant of that structure, let alone the owner. It is simply the caretaker. Surely, the landlord, the people of Canada, have a right to know what the caretaker has been doing to keep the property in good condition. That is all we are asking as the representatives of the people who in fact own this business.
We have had reports from two of the inspectors who have been on this property, and they have not found the condition of the property very good. We are asking that other inspectors who have been there also be permitted to give their reports, and that, in any place where it has not been examined, it be still further examined.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a pertinent question? Was it not during the time that the hon. gentleman was premier of Ontario that he denied to the house and to the country the Hope report?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That interjection and the
applause which followed it indicate the kind of red herring that those on the other side seek to draw across the trail. The Hope report, as the hon. member well knows, was neither completed nor presented to the government of Ontario until long after I had left the legislature of that province. In fact I can only express regret that the hon. member in this case does not display that attention to detail which I admit he did display
The Budget-Mr. Drew while he was also directly associated with provincial activities in Ontario.
This is simply a further example of the apparent necessity for continued emphasis on the fact that we are trying to get assurances from the government that this will be dealt with in a way that will produce some positive results. It is very noticeable that in the presidential addresses of almost every bank in Canada this year emphasis has been placed upon the need for taking whatever steps can be taken to increase economy in the administration of government for the purpose of checking inflation. In several of those speeches it was pointed out that while it is not easy to effect these economies, particularly as between departments, nevertheless real efforts should be made to cut unnecessary government spending and to save wherever possible by the introduction of efficient methods.
The ordinary housekeeper has to establish her budget on the basis of what she is allowed to spend. She does not set up her budget on the basis of some arbitrary figure that she thinks she would like to spend. If the ordinary housewife in Canada followed the same practices that are being followed by this government at this time there is not one of us in this house who does not realize the unhappy results which would follow in an ordinary household where that practice was adopted.
We are seeing before us the very real dangers inherent in the centralization of taxation and government power. Every one of us here knows perfectly well that, the closer spending is to the people, the more care is exercised in relation to the spending of money. Those who have had experience in the municipal field know perfectly well how carefully people in those communities watch the expenditure of every dollar, and how responsible members in those municipal councils are to the demands for economies which are made by the people, who see how the money is being spent.
In the provincial legislature, business is still closer to the people than it is here, although not so close as in most municipal councils. That is one reason why all of us should watch what is going on, and watch it very carefully. The year before last 77 cents out of every tax dollar was collected by this government, leaving only 23 cents for provincial governments and municipal councils to carry out their extremely important tasks.
Now, if this trend had been changed, there would be some reason for encouragement. But it has not been changed. The percentage
2966	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew [DOT]collected by the central government is still higher. Last year it was 78 cents out of every tax dollar that was collected by the central government, leaving only 22 cents out of the tax dollar available for the provinces and the municipalities.
This concentration of spending power not only encourages the reckless use of power by the government which has it, but also it withdraws from the supervision of the people the expenditure of their own money. Some of those people who are today feeling the impact of taxation are inclined to feel a sense of detachment in regard to expenditures by the central government.
That is another reason why we should economize. That is another reason why there should be a conference where there could be laid a foundation for the kind of readjustment in taxation which has been demanded by the provinces for several years.
The fact is that this concentration of power is no accident. It is part of the policy of this government that it should get as much power into its own hands as possible. This government gives lip service to our constitution, but it has done more violence to constitutional rights than any government in the history of this country. In fact it is the first government in the history of Canada that has denied the principle that the British North America Act is a solemn pact, which represents the agreement between those who joined to make this country a great nation.
This government regards our written constitution as a mere scrap of paper to be brushed aside whenever the government decides that it is convenient to by-pass parliament, and the provincial legislatures, and to *operate by order in council-which can more accurately be described as government by dictate.	.
The present trend is one which will concern every Canadian interested in our federal system. There is another reason for great caution at this time. This government has not been prepared to recognize that, both in the domestic field and in the external field of business, everything we produce carries with it a hidden load of taxation, and a heavy load at that.
How many Canadians realize that at this time an automobile bought in Canada and made in Canada carries with it a load of government taxes, which, in total, amounts to more than the total amount paid to those who actually worked in making that automobile? And yet that is a fact. And that situation is being repeated in other cases.


This is the load of taxation, which does not appear as part of the price tag, but which is placed on automobiles, washing machines, electrical equipment, and many other things. It is something that is not only added to the burden of our own people, but is also having a very important effect upon our trade with other nations, and will have that effect in years ahead. It applies to agricultural products as well. In the case of every bushel of wheat, every pound of meat, every pound of cheese, and everything else we export, or seek to export, there is thrown in a burden of taxation either upon our own people or upon people who are asked to buy those products.
And when we hear that one of the difficulties we are encountering now in selling our products to certain markets is the fact that they cannot afford to buy, how often is the simple reality faced that one of the reasons they sometimes cannot afford to buy is the fact that our products are carrying such a heavy load of taxation imposed by this government?
No one would suggest for one moment that we can operate without taxes. But because of these facts we do say that this government should give us some assurance that some step will be taken to reduce costs, wherever that can be done. Some of us can remember events after the first world war which should be in the minds of all of us today. Many of us will remember how easy it was to sell products of all kinds in the markets of the world, in the years immediately after the first world war. That condition arose because of the destruction of producing plants in so many countries. We also remember how that changed.
The same thing has happened in the years following the second world war. We are now entering a period of extremely keen competition in export markets. We have hardly realized how fast the industrial recovery has been in some of those countries. The two most important industrial competitors outside of this continent-that is, outside of our western associates in the last war-are Germany and Japan. The figures are striking, when one examines what has happened elsewhere. For instance, in 1952 industrial production in West Germany, in physical volume, was 52 per cent above their pre-war industrial production. The physical volume of industrial production in Japan last year was 29 per cent above their pre-war industrial level.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is Canada?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is something the hon. member can speak about when his time comes to speak. I am pointing out that

this very, rapid increase in countries which were devastated by war indicates what is likely to happen this year, next year and in following years when you consider the measure of recovery in such a comparatively short time since they got back to the rebuilding of their industrial plants. We have taken the position that we welcome these nations into the community of free nations. If we do, then of necessity we must accept their competition. If we accept their competition, then we must face that competition on the basis of price as well as on the basis of quality.
We know that both the countries I have mentioned, as well as other countries, are not carrying today anything like the load of taxation that they carried in the years before the war. It is perfectly well known that, until those countries undertake the building up of military establishments in the common defence of the freedom which they now share, their taxes are bound to be lower than ours. Mr. Speaker, I desire for a short time to discuss the problem of Cuba, and the beet sugar industry in Canada-in fact, the sugar industry in Canada as a whole.
Let it be known at once that I bear no ill will in any way toward Cuba or any other country whatsoever. My object in speaking this afternoon is merely to clarify a situation which in the minds of a good many people in Canada is rather confused. Let us be a good neighbour to Cuba, but let us do it in an orderly way. Let us not pay too much for the whistle of being a good neighbour. Let us help Cuba to help herself. I think that is the attitude adopted generally today by all people engaged in both the beet sugar and the cane sugar industry of Canada.
First may I discuss for a few moments Cuba as an actuality and as a potentiality in the international trade situation of the world, and particularly in the matter of sugar.
Cuba is a great potential asset or a fearful potential liability to the world, and ultimately to herself. She is somewhat like a child playing with matches in a nitroglycerin plant. Cuba had an experience-bitter enough-in the early thirties, which will illustrate to her the truth of what I have just said.
What are Cuba's advantages in the matter of trading in sugar today? There are many. Cuba is a relatively low-cost producer. Rated among all the producers of the world she would, I think, be one of the lowest-cost producers. The United States tariff commission between 1929 and 1932 conducted a study of the cost of production of a pound of sugar in all major geographical sources from which the United States was drawing her sugar supply at that time. They found the costs in certain sugar producing areas to be the following: Louisiana, 5-5 cents a pound; Cuba, 2-7 cents; the Philippine islands, 3-5 cents; continental beet sugar in the United States,

3-1 cents; Puerto Rico, 4-1 cents and the Hawaiian islands, 4 [DOT] 1 cents.
I believe it will be agreed that among these are some of the cheapest producers, potentially, to be found anywhere. Unfortunately, so far as I have been able to find, there are no more recent data available, resulting from what we might call a thoroughly reliable and authentic study. The figures I have just given are quoted in "The Sugar Problem of the United States", issued by the Chamber of Commerce of the United States at Washington, D C., in 1941.
Then Cuba is the world's largest single producer of sugar, producing about one-sixth of the entire world crop. She produces about 6 million to 8 million tons of a total world crop of between 36 million and 38 million tons. She exports all but about 200,000 tons, which she retains for consumption. This shows that she has a considerable amount of sugar to play around with in the world markets.
Cuban refineries can turn out annually over 1,500,000 tons of refined granulated sugar, enough to supply, twice over, the entire annual consumption of Canada. This shows what Canadian refineries are up against. This means obviously that unless Canada takes effective measures to regulate refined sugar imports Cuba could in a very short time utterly destroy all Canadian sugar producers, both cane and beet.
Cuba's method of controlling domestic prices is another tremendous advantage to that country. With her method of control, Cuban exports are simply irresistible where an economy relatively free, such as that in Canada, attempts to maintain itself.
Cuban policy respecting the United States has been such that she must go into United States markets regardless of cost. That has been her policy for a long time. In order to get into the United States market she will reduce her costs, on paper, to the point at which she can enter United States markets. This was the case particularly before 1932-33.
The chairman of the United States tariff commission in a letter to the president of the United States dated April 11, 1933, said:
The situation in Cuba, which is the chief competing foreign country, is such that the higher the American tariff may be, the lower are the costs of producing sugar in Cuba.
Cuba must fix the price at which she sells sugar at a point which will enable her product to enter the American market.
I presume the same thing applies with respect to Canada, when she sees fit to enter the Canadian market. As an example of Cuba's methods, let us turn to what happened in 1952. To avoid anti-dumping laws Cuba
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore set each month an arbitrary price at which their raw sugar, and presumably refined sugar, would be sold for home consumption. For August, 1952, this price was fixed at $3,505 per hundred. This price, plus the refining margin of $1 to $1.18 which they are content to take, but concerning which I am a little doubtful that it can be scientifically established, brought their f.o.b. price to $4.69. Their sale price in Canada was apparently above this at all times. Consequently they could not be accused of dumping according to Canadian law. For September, 1952, the arbitrary raw price was fixed at $3,407 per hundred. Thus again they sidestepped the anti-dumping law.
Then, too, Cuba is in a preferred export position. This is expressed by some by saying that she produces under an umbrella, which is the United States. The United States quota system assures to Cuba the benefit of her full tariff preference plus an additional substantial premium. The United States quota system also guarantees Cuba a market for a substantial amount of sugar, enough to stabilize Cuba's sugar situation. This fact puts Cuba in the preferred export position I have mentioned, enabling her to do what in effect is dumping, although she can so manage her domestic price structure as to evade, on artifically produced technicalities, anti-dumping laws of any country in which Cuba chooses to sell her sugar. May I read the words of an eminent authority on sugar named Frank C. Lowry, as they appear in the Willett and Gray "Weekly Statistical Sugar Trade Journal" of January 24, 1946 at page 37. He says:
Under the quotas, a two-price system for the same article was created in Cuban sugar. Any surplus that could not be shipped to the United States was "dumped" on the so-called world market at the expense of other producers who did not enjoy the protection of the United States quota umbrella. In no small degree this contributed to the gradual decline in world values during the late thirties, making it impossible for the less favoured areas to pay labour more than 25 cents a day. Values in the United States also sagged until the complaint was heard that the market had been "stabilized at the bottom." It will be noted that the new system did not bring the millennium.
That quotation has considerable significance, as all hon. members will recognize. The results that Cuba was able to produce in respect of Canada were clearly demonstrated in the years 1930 and 1931, until in 1932 a minimum price of $2.30 a hundred in place of origin was imposed by Canada for tariff purposes, a matter which I shall discuss in more detail as I continue my speech.
Again, Cuba is in a most potent refined sugar position. Not only does she produce raw sugar in great abundance, but she is

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore now in a position to produce refined sugar also in great abundance. The United States refined sugar quota of 375,000 tons annually to Cuba has perpetuated the sugar refining industry of that country. Cuba's sugar refining capacity is now more than four times her United States refined sugar quota of 375,000 tons a year. The resultant over-quota surplus of refined sugar can be disposed of by Cuba at prices which have no rational relation at all to current prices of raws. Cuba can buy up raws cheaply wherever there happens to be a distress sale among island producers, and either channel them into Canada as raws or refine them and then channel them into this country.
Cuba's production in 1952 was 8 million short tons, at least 2 million tons in excess of possible world demand. By that I do not mean world physical demand but world financial demand, meaning world ability to buy sugar and pay for it. Cuba has set aside
1,750,000	long tons of raw sugar for what they call their stabilization reserve. This they plan to feed into the market over the next five years.
This is enough to show any realistic member of the house that for Canada to turn over her home market for refined sugar with no restriction or regulation on Cuba is to commit suicide for our sugar industry.
I should like to discuss for a few minutes the sub-topic of Cuba and the Canadian beet sugar industry since world war I, and give an outline of what Canadian governments have done about it. Between 1925 and early 1932, the time of the establishment of the $2.30 minimum price in the land of origin for tariff purposes, which occurred on January 27 and 30, 1932, the way was clear for Cuban exports of refined sugar into Canada. To use a wrestling expression, no hold was barred. Cuba was granted permission to come into Canada at will. What happened as a result? Cuban refined entered Canada during those years in the following amounts:

In 1932 the amount declined to 40,000 because of the imposition of the minimum and in 1933, after the minimum got into full action, none was imported.
The next period in our relations with Cuba with respect to sugar runs from 1933 to 1939

inclusive. No sugar was shipped into Canada because of the $2.30 minimum price.
From 1939 to 1951 what happened? There were no sugar exports to Canada because Cubans were able to market their extra sugar without bothering Canada, or it may be that their sugar was shut out as the result of the activities of the sugar controller. The picture is a bit blurred after the appointment of a controller in Canada. It is not easy for us to find out exactly what occurred. In addition, the United States was becoming alarmed concerning her sugar supply, and she drew quite heavily upon Cuba. The result was that so far as I have found we have no record of specific imports of Cuban refined sugar during that period.
Early in 1952 Cuba began shipping refined sugar into Canada. What was the reason Cuba did this? As I shall develop later, up to that time world sugar producing areas had not fully recovered from the devastation brought about by war. Consequently the world's supply was inadequate, causing a good demand for Cuban sugar.
Now, what has Canada done since 1925 in respect of Cuba and Cuban sugar? Between 1925 and January 27, 1932, Canada did nothing specifically to protect the Canadian sugar refining industry, both beet and cane, against Cuban refined imports. On January 27, 1932, order in council P.C. 181 was passed authorizing the Minister of National Revenue to fix the value for duty of refined granulated sugar. On January 30, 1932, appraiser's bulletin No. 3815 fixed the $2.30 value. Between January 30, 1932, and on or after November 20, 1939, when appraiser's bulletin No. 3815 was cancelled, Canada did effectively shut out Cuban refined from the Canadian market, regardless of wartime conditions or any other conditions.
Between on or after November 20, 1939 and the cessation of wartime controls on sugar on April 1, 1950, the Canadian government in a way protected from external sources the Canadian sugar refining industry through the agency of wartime sugar control.
We now come to the great mishap. The Canadian government, upon abolishing wartime controls on April 1, 1950, neglected to restore the $2.30 minimum or any other minimum, and neglected to take any other measure to protect the Canadian sugar industry, both cane and beet, against Cuban refined. This is the move on the part of the Canadian government which has caused the importation of Cuban sugar this year to the extent that it has greatly embarrassed the beet sugar industry and, I presume, greatly alarmed the cane refining industry also.

For a year or so there was no active danger because the world sugar producing industry, as I said a moment ago, had not sufficiently recovered from the damage of world war II and Cuba could sell elsewhere to good advantage.
In 1951 the Canadian government made an agreement to buy 75,000 tons of raw from Cuba in each of three years, apparently making no stipulation as to Cuban refined. Just as soon as Canada made an agreement with Cuba to buy raw, that probably was taken by the Cubans as an indication that Canada was prepared to buy any amount of sugar now that Cuba had to offer, provided it was refined. The result was that they began to exploit the possibilities of the situation.
By 1952 world production had nearly enough recovered to cause Cuba to desire to sell refined in Canadian markets. Still Canada took no defensive measures. In early 1952 Cuban refined again began to come into Canada.
I should like now to read two or three quotations from the sugar refining industry memorandum on behalf of the Atlantic Sugar Refineries Limited, the Acadia Sugar Refining Company Limited, and the St. Lawrence Refineries Limited. This was their submission to the tariff inquiry which, as I recall it, was conducted in 1939. It was a most important inquiry. I read from page 55 of their submission.
The entry of tropical refined sugar into the world export market in 1926 was an event of major importance to the refining industries of the temperate zones and constitutes the greatest threat to the latter that has arisen for many years. Because of its size and phenomenal growth the Cuban industry may be selected for special discussion but the development of refining industries in other raw sugar producing countries carries the same threat to the Canadian industry.
There is the declaration of those three great cane sugar refineries in Canada, indicating genuine alarm because of the possibilities implicit in Cuba by reason of her development of her cane refining industry.
From page 58 of their document I read as follows:
It was realized from the outset that the Cuban exports were being dumped on the Canadian market but the difficulty of proof as regards each shipment prevented any adequate remedy. In their anxiety to find markets for their extra quota accumulations of raw sugar, raw sugar was charged into the refining operation at prices substantially below the prevailing price for raws in the world markets. This practice was established to the satisfaction of the Canadian government, and finally in January, 1932, an order in council was passed under section 43 of the Customs Act fixing a valuation for duty purposes on refined sugar under the general tariff of $2.30 per 100 pounds, United States funds. As a result a dumping duty
2975
The Budget

Mr. Blackmore was established amounting to the sum by which the price to the Canadian buyer was less than $2.30 per 100 pounds, United States funds; provided however that this duty should not as provided in tariff item 134 exceed three-quarters of a cent per pound. This had the effect of stopping the influx of Cuban refined.
Our Liberal friends who talk so much nonsense about the Conservatives under Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, for whom I have no brief at all except my desire to see Liberals be decently truthful, will be interested to note what is said in that statement concerning what caused the Conservative government in 1932 to impose the $2.30 minimum. I read from page 65:
There remains one further criticism of the fixed valuation that calls for careful study. It is alleged that even were it abolished Cuban refined could not now compete in Canada and consequently if it has no value to the refining industry why not repeal it? It is quite true that price levels in Canada today are such as to prevent the importation of Cuban refined based on the published quotation on such refined f.o.b. Cuba. These figures (bated on quotations received on June 6, 1939) work out as follows:
Cuban export price f.o.b. seaport ___$1.80
Freight to New York (sea train)	16
Handling	04
Freight to Toronto (canal)	24
Duty under Item 134	 1.89
Duty on bag	03
Import tax	n
Total without dumping duty	 $4.27
As compared with the Canadian refiners' price in Toronto of $4.23.
While it is quite true, as the example shows, that the Canadian refiner is not taking any price advantage from the fixed valuation-
May I interrupt there to point out a very serious matter. The other day someone said that he trembled to think what the Canadian cane refineries would do if certain conditions were now established. Here there was found no disposition on the part of the Canadian refineries to take advantage of the $2.30 minimum.
-he is deriving the intended benefit of increased volume output resulting from the exclusion of the dumped product, but there is more to the situation than that and the following considerations should be given due weight in a study of question:
(a)	The danger of an influx of Cuban refined into Canada on a purely dumping basis is greater today than it was in 1932 for three reasons:
(i)	The capacity of the Cuban refined industry has greatly increased.
(ii)	Having an assured market in the United States for a large output at prices above the cost of production, the Cuban industry is so much more enabled to dump her "over-quota" sugar.
(iii)	Her refining capacity is still double her actual production.
(b)	At any time it is possible for the Cuban refiner to acquire raws at substantially less than world prices and to sell for export refined sugar at prices very little in advance of the world's raw prices. Such competition is at all times threatening and would, without any reasonable doubt, develop if the fixed valuation were abolished.
2976	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
(c)	Removal of the fixed valuation would be construed In Cuba as an invitation to enter the Canadian market just as surely as a minor reduction in the spread provided by the American tariff in 1930 gave Cuba's exports to the United States a tremendous impetus. Potentially at the present time the Cuban refined sugar industry is capable of capturing the whole of the Canadian market. Destruction through price cutting of the Canadian industry would undoubtedly exclude from Canada all empire raws, nor could empire refined hope to compete against the Cuban granulated. The only portion of the Canadian trade that Cuba would not obtain under present circumstances would be the special packaged goods and the varieties other than granulated which are of very minor volume in the total. Such a condition of affairs would become imminent and would develop as soon as the fixed valuation disappeared.
We have lived to see the fulfilment of the gloomy forecast made in this submission.
It needs to be borne in mind that Canada has certain commitments with various members of the commonwealth in respect of the buying of their sugar. It is an important thing at this point for us to know that we in Canada have bought sugar from a great number of different sources. May I just run through the names of the countries from which we bought sugar during the years 1928 to 1937:
South Africa, Australia, Fiji, British Guiana, Barbados, San Domingo, Jamaica, Cuba, Trinidad, other British West Indies, British East Indies, Belgium, The Netherlands, British East Africa.
That is enough to show that we have no right to allow Cuba to monopolize the refined granulated cane sugar market in Canada. Obviously something must be done to regulate the imports of refined sugar into Canada. Unregulated importations of Cuban refined and raw sugar could in a very short time utterly ruin and wipe out all Canadian sugar production, both cane and beet, both raw and refined. That would mean a dangerous loss to Canada and an extremely expensive one. Something must be done to regulate by statute the importation of refined cane sugar from Cuba and all other countries.
It will be my aim some time in the future when opportunity presents itself to outline the history of Cuba and the United States in respect of sugar, and indicate how different has been the policy adopted by the United States in dealing with this Cuban sugar question from 1933 forward from that which Canada has adopted. The United States has used a series of sugar acts. The first act was passed in 1934; the second act was passed in 1937, and the third act was passed in 1948. United States policy was adjusted to the changing conditions which prevailed at those three dates.
Under those acts the United States guaranteed to accept a certain quota of sugar from

Cuba and from each of the offshore possessions of the United States such as the Virgin islands, Puerto Rico, the Hawaiian islands, and from the Philippine islands. She guaranteed to accept such amounts at such prices as would allow generally for all the production of which her own cane producers were capable, and all the production of which her beet sugar producers were capable. At the same time she produced a fine stabilizing effect upon the markets in these other countries I have named.
As I said, I hope to discuss this matter at some future time and to indicate to this country the kind of policy which I think it would be advisable for us to adopt as regards this whole matter of sugar.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think one of the finest cartoonists we have in Canada is Ron Smith of the Ottawa Journal. On Friday or Saturday last he had a delightful cartoon in that paper which depicted the House of Commons with two pipe lines flowing from it, one going east and west and the other going north and south. It was headed, "Natural Canadian Gas now flowing at full capacity. Pre-election Pipe Line Unlimited." The east and west pipe was indicated with Victoria at the one end and Halifax at the other. I take it that the assumption we have to take from this is that the great island and newest province is not to be influenced by Canadian gas. However, there is a warning that we have to keep in mind, that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is planning to visit the island within the next day or so. Possibly that pipe line will have to be redrawn following his visit. I am not sure of that, but would not be too surprised.
There is an old Chinese proverb which says that a government is like the wind and the people like the grass, that when the wind blows the grass must bend. Well, this government has shown in its administration that it believes implicitly in the truth of that proverb. How otherwise can be explained the attitude of members of the Liberal party in this house when they have had clearly demonstrated to them that there is waste and extravagance as proved by various reports, not only the report of Mr. Currie but the report of the Auditor General himself.
I do not want to flog a beaten horse, because certain horses have been flogged quite a lot; but I cannot help comparing the infamous horses of Petawawa with the famous wooden horse of Troy. Incidentally, I heard only today that the wooden horse of Troy was on the payroll of Helen. The real difference between that horse and the others

we have been hearing about is that the one was wooden while the others were really alive. I understand that following the original disclosures as to these horses one senior Liberal member in the house told a newspaper correspondent, "I hope they stop these nags; otherwise they will toe galloping from coast to coast." There can be no question about it, these horses are galloping and they are galloping pretty fast.
When speaking of horses one instantly thinks of grass, and that brings me back to my original remark about the government being the wind and the people being the grass. I am afraid that no matter what explanations are given in this house or elsewhere, the government can puff and blow as long as it wishes but it will never blow those horses down. Like Johnnie Walker they will keep on going strong, and like the wooden horse of Troy they will destroy the Liberal party.
You will remember that at the time that horse was introduced to the Trojans a famous philosopher inside the walls said, "Beware the Greeks bearing gifts." These horses were brought as a gift. We would never have known about these horses except as a gift. I can assure members of the Liberal party that from what I hear they had better beware of this gift.
Back in the old days in what was then the dominion of Newfoundland we had our own government. There was a well-known and famous Canadian lawyer who had had quite considerable success in the political life of Newfoundland. When he left Newfoundland he said that Newfoundlanders were too green to burn. May I say that is an extremely fortunate situation because otherwise, with the hot winds that have been blowing since we became part of this great dominion, we would have been long ago burned by the unnecessarily high taxation to which we, like the rest of Canada, have been subjected. We have been seared, but we have not been long enough in the union to be burned completely.
Why do I mention this matter? For one purpose and one purpose only. I am going to deal with only two provincial matters. The first is a matter that I have been raising ever since I originally came into this house in 1949. I began on September 22, 1949 and repeatedly, at each opportunity I have had, ending with April 30 of last year, I have raised this matter of the necessity for a revision of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada. I have pointed out to hon. members of this house the necessity for adequate revision of the financial terms of union.
68108-189i
The Budget-Mr. Higgins
That necessity still exists, and is even more apparent today than it was in April of last year. I will not go into the reason; I think it is obvious to most people. We had a $45 million surplus at the time of union, and now we have had to borrow money. It is quite obvious that we shall have to have this royal commission that was made part of the terms of union; and I submit that it should be constituted at the earliest possible moment, Mr. Speaker, so that it may be put to work.
The party of which I have the honour to be a member, at the time this matter was originally discussed back in 1948, stated its position clearly and unequivocally, namely that it was opposed to the set-up of the terms of union. The Liberal party, through the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), at that time stated'-I cannot give the exact date but it was in 1948, during the final discussion- that even if this royal commission which was to be set up brought in a favourable recommendation with respect to adequate revision of the terms of union, nevertheless, in spite of that fact, no guarantee could be given that the terms of union would be revised.
I bring that matter forward, Mr. Speaker, because I feel that the time is rapidly approaching when, whether we wish it or not and whether those in the Liberal party-my colleagues from Newfoundland especially- agree with me or not, we shall have to have that royal commission set up. It is past the joking stage altogether, and it is altogether past the stage of arguing in a political sense. It is such a complete necessity now that the commission be set up that I think all hon. members from Newfoundland will join with me in making that recommendation.
The only other matter that I wish to deal with provincially is the question of the construction of an armoury for the reserve regiments at St. John's and with that I will leave it. Through the kindness of the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), shortly before Christmas we had a meeting in his office and an address was made by the then lieutenant colonel of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment, Lieutenant Colonel O'Driscoll. I have given to various members copies of the address he delivered at that time. I did not have a sufficient number with which to supply all hon. members, but I hope I shall have more within the next few weeks. The gist of Colonel O'Driscoll's remarks was this, and I am quoting now from what he said at the time:
The situation in St. John's today is anything but satisfactory. We are endeavouring to train cadets and reserve force units in buildings belonging to the Royal Canadian Navy which are not at all suitable for training soldiers. This can be confirmed
2978	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Higgins by the area commander and his staff now in St. John's who belong to eastern command.
While the administrative branch is suitably housed, there is no proper armoury lor carrying out training as such. This applies to the three reserve units located there; 166th Field Regiment; 56th (Independent) Royal Engineers; Royal Newfoundland Regiment.
These three units are presently trying to train in a drill hall which was constructed during the last war for the Royal Canadian Navy. This drill hall is not at all suitable, for various reasons, amongst which are:
And he enumerates the reasons.
1.	It has a hardwood floor. This, while satisfactory for training of naval personnel, who have rubber heels on their boots and shoes, is not at all satisfactory for soldiers who have steel hobnails and: heel plates on their boots. It is obvious that they slip and slide over this floor and therefore have no control over army drills.
2.	The acoustics are very bad. This can be verified at any time by properly authorized persons attending parades.
3.	There are no facilities whatsoever for lecture rooms, training rooms, messes, or canteens, et cetera.
4.	There is no proper parade square in the location where these reserve units are training.
Without reading the full paragraph, I may summarize. He says that in the event of mobilization the navy will require the whole property and the army units will have no place available. I am not going to read any more of the memorandum except this last part:
I wish to emphasize-
Says Lieutenant Colonel O'Driscoll.
-in this memorandum the fact that the Royal Newfoundland Regiment is the oldest regiment in Canada. Its history dates back to 1775, when units were recruited in Newfoundland and came to Canada and successfully defended York and other locations against the invasion of American forces. They have no permanent home of their own to house the trophies won in battles or to display their battle honours. There is no esprit de corps to which they can indoctrinate the incoming recruits. Pride of regiment is a paramount feature in recruiting. This has been very well borne out in the last two recruiting drives for Korea and northwest Europe. Without the proper facilities for indoctrination and keeping esprit de corps alive throughout the regiment, it is impossible to keep the interest of these soldiers. Trophies won in the last two wars are now scattered throughout the length and breadth of Newfoundland with no permanent resting place. They should be collected and displayed in their own armoury. Without such trophies it is very difficult indeed to keep the interest of reserve units.
It is very strongly urged that the Minister of National Defence given his earnest consideration to the above proposal. He has visited Newfoundland and inspected reserve units there and expressed himself as being very proud of them.
That is the end of what I wish to read. I wish to emphasize once again-and I am sure that my colleagues from Newfoundland will agree with me-that the necessity for our own armoury is most apparent.

Just for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I wish now to deal with a matter that is possibly not quite as pleasant as those about which I have been speaking up till now.
I refer to a speech that I did not hear but which I read on Saturday. It was made by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Gour). I take the greatest exception not to all he said but to some parts of that speech. The parts that I agree with, I agree with thoroughly. With this particular reference I am in full accord and I am quoting the hon. member's exact words as reported in Hansard of March 13:
What this country needs is good will between races, between provinces, between classes . . .
And later he said:
. . . there can be no good will without justice.
The statement that there can be no good will without justice is the most important part of the whole speech made by the hon. member. I want hon. members on all sides of the house to bear this in mind, for what does the hon. member for Russell say following that? I am rather surprised, knowing him-or at least thinking I know him- because I read an extremely odious comparison drawn by him between the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and made in such a manner that I do not think there can be anybody in this house who will not take exception to it.
I have as high an opinion of the Prime Minister as anybody in this house. I admire the great qualities of his heart and mind. I think he is the finest example we have had for some time of a statesman in Canada.
I agree with all that in every way. But I also say that in my opinion-and it is the opinion of a great many others in this house- the Leader of the Opposition should be regarded in the same light. I am sure the Prime Minister himself would be the first to take exception to such a statement if he had heard it made. It is not because we have a leader of the opposition that he must be spoken of in terms such as those used by the hon. member at that time, and this is the last part of his speech I am going to read. He said:
What a comparison between our Right Hon. Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition; one is qualified to lead and govern our country through the greatest period of prosperity of our history, and the other to remain Leader of the [DOT] Opposition, until the supporters of his party succeed in replacing him, . . .
That is pretty rough, as far as I am concerned.
It is cheap.

I am speaking as a new
.member of this house. I do not believe any hon. member would endorse a remark such as that; but the worst part in the speech of the hon. member-I am sorry he is not here to hear me, because I do not like talking behind a man's back-is yet to come. In the last part of his speech he went even farther and invaded the privacy of the home of my leader. He discussed where and how my leader's children are being educated, and to that I take very great exception indeed, not only ' as a member of this party but as a member of this house. This is what he said as reported at page 2940 of the translation of the hon. member's speech of Friday March 13:
Now my friends, be serious with yourselves, if you are not serious with your electors. The Leader of the Opposition is responsible for this country being ridiculed in Europe since he sends his children to study abroad. This fact was mentioned to me quite often during my trip abroad, when I was fortunate enough to visit ten foreign countries. I was asked whether we had good schools at home. And when I answered there were none better I was told: "That is what we were always told, but how is it that our newspapers spread the news around here that-
Cheap politics.

-the Leader of the Opposition to the Canadian government wants to send his children to study abroad?" In this way he gives the impression that according to him our schools are not modern enough or well prepared enough to educate his children. That would be easier to understand were they older, and had they gone abroad for specialized professional training in European universities. I therefore close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, expressing regrets that our friends overseas are apt to have an entirely false idea of what conditions really are with regard to educational institutions.
That, Mr. Speaker, to me is the cheapest remark I have ever heard in this house. I do not think it is worthy of any hon. member. I hope none of the members listening to me this afternoon were here listening when that remark was made, because the hon. member who made that speech does not deserve any endorsation; in fact he deserves in every way, I suggest to you, to be severely criticized even by his greatest friends. That is all I have to say about that part of his remarks, and I hope he reads what I have said.
I intend to devote the remainder of my time to discussing the two dominant races of Canada. Possibly it may be considered presumptuous on my part to discuss this matter, particularly as I am a new Canadian, but may I say that each of these races has contributed much to Canadian development in the past four centuries. I submit that as a new Canadian, possibly without any of the prejudices that come from living too close to Canadian life, I may be in a better position
The Budget-Mr. Higgins to sum up the fabric of Canadian life and get a clearer perspective and a fresher viewpoint.
This great country of ours has two great racial, cultural and religious traditions; the Roman Catholic culture of old France and the predominantly Protestant culture of the Anglo-Saxon countries. To these shores of course have come people from other lands, each bringing with him his own distinctive contribution to our culture, and each helping to complete the weaving of our national tapestry. I feel certain that the differences in background of our newer citizens, including the citizens of our newest province, will serve not to weaken the nation but to strengthen and enrich Canadian life.
One of the greatest challenges facing Canada today is to secure national unity in the midst of cultural diversity. This is far from impossible of fulfilment, as I see it, Mr. Speaker, for the differences need not separate Canadians but can strengthen Canadian life. Among peoples of different religious background, racial origin, and political beliefs, three most important requirements are necessary, namely tolerance, respect and good will.
We have such a lot in common here in Canada that we should keep emphasizing these things which bring us together rather than those which separate us. If the differences between two peoples are encouraged they may well lead to suspicion, antagonism, prejudice, aye and even actual hatred. They can very well impair our social order, disfigure Canadian life and menace the unity of the national effort not only in war but in peace.
No greater weapons to destroy people can be put into the hands of the communists than racial intolerance and religious bigotry. There should be no doubt in anyone's mind that the supreme problem facing mankind today is the ability of men and women to rise above differences of race, creed and class and live together in peace, friendship and brotherhood.
The answer to the problem is not the stamping out of these differences, but of promoting respect and understanding for these very divergences. It is no good pretending that there are no differences or to endeavour to level them out to a common denominator. What we must do is attempt to develop an understanding and a frank and healthy respect for one another. It is of the greatest importance that we really get to know one another, for ignorance spawns suspicion and hatred. Without knowledge there can be no understanding. You all recall the old statement, "In the night all cats are grey." It
2980	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart might be of course, but I doubt it, that some hon. members would prefer to go along with Charles Lamb who stated that he did not want to get to know the man who lived at the end of the block, for if he knew him he would be denied the luxury of hating him.
That is about all I have to add except to remind all members of the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was so much respected by hon. members, I am sure, and who said:
I love France which has given us life; I love England, which has given us liberty; but the first place in my heart is for Canada, my fatherland, my native country."

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate, particularly to the criticism that has been passed across by the opposition, and I want to go back over the record, to the budget previous to the 1949 election. I found some remarks which were made at that time by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), which I should like to put on the record again. He made a statement with regard to it being a bribery budget, and a short time later he made this statement, which I quote from page 1810 of Hansard of that year.
-the increase of $50 for dependent children is utterly inadequate, and that it should have been $200 as we suggested.
This debate has followed along pretty much the same line, but I did And a statement put on the record at that time that I think should be put on the record again. It will be found on page 2182 of Hansard of March 31, 1949. I might also add, before I quote these remarks, that I think it is his masterpiece. He said:
Of course the minister has the great disadvantage of representing a city riding-and what a disadvantage that is! I told him the other day he was nothing better than a city slicker, but even then I did not know how true it was.
He was speaking of the Minister of Finance. Speaking in the same chamber today the same hon. gentleman made the statement that we should be a little more careful in the language we use in this house. Just what the definition would be of a city slicker I do not know, but these are the words he used, I want you to look back over the record since that time. It is a case of the pot calling the kettle black.
Don't tell anyone in Greenwood that.

But it will be a boomerang, because I know today the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) also represents a city riding. Does he consider himself a city slicker?
I have listened to the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for St.
(Mr. Higgins.]

John's West (Mr. Browne), and I must say that I listened to the most dismal display of. defending the Bennett government that I have ever listened to in my life. That is particularly true of the remarks of the hon. member for St. John's West when, as reported at page 2791 of Hansard, he said:
From a comparison of these things you will see that Canada came out of the depression under the Bennett government better than did any other country in the world.
Might I remind the hon. member for St. John's West that if the Bennett government brought this country out of the depression, then very few Canadians knew anything about it. The record is there for anyone to see. It speaks for itself.
During the dark, dismal and despondent thirties no doubt the hon. member for St. John's West lived very well. He was not a primary producer. Perhaps the way he lived during that period of time would compare favourably with the way he lives today. Living costs at that time were away down. One dollar then would buy as much as three dollars would buy today. So no doubt he lived very well. But I doubt if many of his countrymen were in that same position. I believe he would have found the same condition prevailing in Newfoundland that prevailed at that time in Canada. And I might add that it would appear that the efforts made to improve conditions in Newfoundland compared very favourably with the disgraceful record of the methods used by the Bennett administration in Canada.
At that time there were young men in government camps getting 20 cents a day and producing nothing. Can anyone defend an administration which would support such things as that? Young men were taken off the street, to get them out of the cities. There were things that could have been done. There were many things we needed in Canada at that time, and those young men could have been employed profitably for this country. But they were given 20 cents a day and hidden in work camps to keep them off the streets.
Why do you not get a little schoolhouse for that claptrap? That is where it would be most appropriate.

I am pleased that the hon. member has mentioned that. I wish to tell him the story about his provincial record. He sat in the provincial legislature of New Brunswick from 1925 to 1935. After promising the people of that province old age pensions, what happened during the 1930 election? It was the grand betrayal of all time, when his party circulated application forms to every clergyman in the province,

telling them that right after the election they would have their old age pensions. He sat there, but there was no pension paid at that time. And, let me add, during that period of time we paid our proportionate share of the federal revenue to pay for old age pensions in other provinces. And that gentleman today styles himself as the champion of the pensioners in this country. That is his record. He asked for it, and he has got it. And may I add that when they were asked why they could not pay the old age pension they said they did not have the money. Well, a Liberal government came into power in 1935, and within 10 months the money was found to pay old age pensions.
May I ask where that Liberal government is today?
I will come to that in a moment. I like to answer questions; let them come, and I will answer them.
We have listened to that sort of thing before.

That is your record as it stands today in the province of New Brunswick, and it cannot be denied.
I shall return now to remarks made by the hon. member for St. John's West and the hon. member for Greenwood. Today the hon. member for Greenwood put on the record the approach made by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and his government to various questions, and he referred to the way he handled the situation with regard to the tariff.
Mishandled.

May I say to the
hon. member through you, Mr. Speaker, that the same thing happened to the old age pension bill in New Brunswick. It was hidden away for ten years. Then when we got a Liberal government in 1935 it was dusted off and put into effect. Policies are never any good if they are just pigeonholed. You have to put them into operation.
The hon. member for St. John's West went on to try to make it appear that the Canadian people were happy with the conditions that prevailed between 1930 and 1935; and the hon. member for Greenwood has said that the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was ready to put the agreements into effect. We all know that these agreements were very beneficial to every Canadian citizen; but the Bennett government was still endeavouring to blast its way into the markets of the world.
The Right Hon. Mr. King did this, and without explosives; and he did it in a very
16, 1953
The Budget-Mr. A. W. Stuart short time after the 1935 election. In other words the Right Hon. Mr. King accomplished in a few weeks the things that the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett could not do in five years. That is all on the record for anyone to read; and it is a good example of the difference in the approach to vital questions by Tory and Liberal administrations.
I should now like to direct my remarks for a few moments to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), and the contribution he made to this debate. In his contribution he made a most feeble effort to defend the Tory legislature in New Brunswick which has already broken every election promise it made, and it made plenty of them.
At this point let me say that he stated the tobacco tax as applied in New Brunswick today is exactly the same as it was under the McNair administration. I worked for that particular branch of government for two years. I audited a good many tobacco accounts, and I know that never since 1940, at the time this regulation was put into effect, has the tobacco tax of New Brunswick been more than 10 per cent of the retail value.
I will challenge any member in this house to show where at any time that tax was ever more than 10 per cent. But the hon. member for Gloucester says the tax today is exactly the same as it was under the McNair administration. I suggest to him that I will use the same terms that the opposition has used in respect of the 2 per cent increase in the sales tax, and say that this is an increase of 33 J per cent. That is the tobacco tax in New Brunswick. That is what the people are paying. It is 33J per cent more than it was under the McNair administration.
That was the new government that was going to cut taxes to the bone. They were going to have a budget that would show a surplus; and the first move they make we find that they are increasing taxation. The hon. member brought into his remarks the fact that the sales tax was taken off drugs, and that this would amount to about $200,000. Well, let me say to the hon. member for Gloucester that if he would give me the increase of 33J per cent on tobacco, he could have the decrease on drugs, because I would be away ahead of him.
The hon. member also tried to indicate in his remarks that there had been no change in the tobacco tax. I want the people of New Brunswick to know that there has been a change. The change is the same as when there was a 2 per cent increase in the sales

The Budget*-Mr. A. W. Stuart tax; it is a 33 J per cent increase. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gave the people a break and the tobacco companies co-operated, taking another 2 cents off the price. Then the provincial government in New Brunswick increased the tobacco tax, instead of decreasing it. That is the fact, and the people in New Brunswick know it as well as I do. Mr. Speaker, since I am entering the debate at this stage it is not my intention to deal at any length with the aspects of the current budget, as many thousands of words have been placed on Hansard and everything that can be said pro and con is now on the record. I do wish, however, to make a few observations before I speak on one or two matters of concern to the maritimes and to the constituency of Northumberland.
This year's budget is a national production budget, made possible by Canada's rapidly expanding prosperity, which shows an increase of over a billion dollars in the value of goods and services produced in Canada in 1952-53. The predicted surplus for 1953-54 is estimated at $11 million compared with $48 million in 1952-53. Revenues for 1953-54 are estimated at a record of $4,473 million, and expenditures at an estimated $4,462 million. The principle followed that revenues depend not only on the tax rates but also on the amounts in which the taxes are applied is a sound one, and a principle that is well recognized by the Canadian people.

The tax deductions include an imposing list of concessions at a time when our defence burden is very heavy. Persons who are not in the income tax brackets, as well as persons who pay income tax, find relief in this year's budget. Canada's financial policy is highlighted by the fact that our country's national debt, greatly increased during the depression years of the thirties and the cost of world war II, has in the last seven years been reduced by $2,350 million, saving to the people of Canada $63 million annually in interest charges alone. Canada's finances are in capable hands. The record over the past few years, since the termination of world war II, stands out in our history. Canada leads the world in this phase of government. This is a record every Canadian should be proud of.
To the majority of citizens our fiscal policy is a matter of surplus or deficit. Comparisons are made by the individual as to the amount of tax he pays in relation to the services he and members of his family receive; a comparison as to his standard of living of today with what it was previously; a study of the social security and other services now enjoyed and the realization that our NATO and United Nations commitments must be met. In brief, the average citizen asks himself: What do I get for the taxes I pay? Would I wish to pay less tax, direct or indirect, and do without some, or all, of the many services now enjoyed under our present taxation system, and withhold our support in the struggle for world peace and leave the burden with the other free nations?
