Mr. Speaker, when listening to the budget

speech my first reaction was that it was a budget that would, by and large, satisfy everybody, and immediately I had the thought that there would be no occasion for me to enter into the debate. However, when I heard or read the remarks of those who have been criticizing the budget, I changed my mind and decided I would take some part in the discussion.
During the course of this debate there has been much effort on the part of the opposition to label the budget with a slogan. The official opposition has termed it an election budget, a sunset budget, a mink coat budget, while the C.C.F. see it as a rich man's budget, a capitalist budget, and even a good Tory budget. They even describe the opposition amendment as semi-socialist. These contradictions indicate that the opposition parties are having difficulty in finding any ground for sound criticism of the budget, so they necessarily resort to catch phrases in the hope one such phrase will catch the ear of the public.
In the Guysb'oro County Advocate of February 27, a newspaper which has never been noticeably favourable to the present administration, there appears a cartoon which to my mind offers a more fair-minded description of the budget. In this cartoon industry and labour are using a cross-cut saw to cut yet another length from the tax log, while a third person, obviously our genial Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), sits on the log and observes that he would not have been able to obtain this last tax cut for the Canadian people were it not for the combined effort of industry and labour. This bears out the admonition given to Canadians over and over again by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of Finance and others that increased production and co-operation between industry and labour is the only way by which Canadians can hope for lower taxes while the international situation remains uncertain and defence costs continue high.
Facts speak much louder than theories, and when we note that our gross national product has increased from $16J billion in 1949 to nearly $23 billion in 1952 we must realize that this is the explanation of the tax reductions that have been made and, in all fairness, give credit where credit is due, to the Canadian people who have brought about this increase in production, and also to the Canadian government for its wise leadership and skilful handling of the nation's finances, which have earned this social dividend to which the Minister of Finance has referred.
No government or minister of finance could or should ever expect to fully satisfy the

opposition, but it is interesting to note what the people of other countries think.
A few days ago the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lesage) quoted several press releases indicating how other nations envy the financial achievements of our government under a Liberal administration. In the Halifax Herald of February 25 appeared the following from the Dublin Daily Irish Independent, commenting on the Canadian budget relief:
"How are such miracles performed?"
Mr. Laidlaw, director of the extension department of St. Francis Xavier university in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, who has recently returned from Europe, after a three months' travelling fellowship awarded by the Carnegie corporation, has this to say concerning Canada's growing prestige in Europe:
Scores of educated Europeans have their eyes on Canada, and Canadians do not appreciate our present prestige in the old world.
In the face of glowing tributes from other sources, one can understand why the opposition is compelled to resort to such feeble or weak criticism of the budget, a criticism which they feel is the duty of the opposition. I would like to make a few observations on those phases of the budget, and of the minister's financial survey, which apply more particularly to the economy of the maritimes and are of special interest to our people.
I was pleased to note that all the changes in the tariff were downward. The people of the maritime provinces, and especially those engaged in farming and fishing, have suffered a great deal from the high tariff system imposed on this country by previous Conservative governments. High tariffs always operate to raise the prices of the things we have to buy, denying us the opportunity of buying on even terms with the people of the United States and other countries. Such a system also tends to close foreign markets for our exports. If we do not buy the products of other countries they, of course, will not and cannot buy the commodities which we have to sell.
In this connection I wish to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for his firm and enlightened stand on the sugar business. Cuba in the past, and right now, is a good market for Canadian products. Cuba's principal export product is sugar, but we cannot sell our fish, potatoes, wheat and other commodities in Cuba if we do not give Cuba a fair chance to sell sugar in Canada. Protectionist interests in central Canada wanted the government to shut out Cuban sugar. There was a threat that if the government did not shut out Cuban sugar, the refineries would close down. Well, the

Some years ago our government took the tariff off the main items of farm machinery. There was a great outcry that the farm machinery manufacturers would be ruined. But they were not ruined. They are doing better than ever, and our farmers can now buy farm implements without paying either a duty or a duty-enhanced price. The same applied to items used in the fishing industry. Many were made duty-free prior to this year. Now we have the duty removed from engines for fishing boats, and wire rope and cable; and additional items of interest to .farmers will now enter the country duty free.
The government's policy of reducing duties on the implements of production in the primary industries, fishing, farming, mining and lumbering, is sound. This gives producers a better chance to compete in the world markets.
The world is far from free of trade restrictions, tariffs, embargoes and quotas, but we can take pride in the fact that right through the picture Canada has been a leader in pressing for the removal of barriers to trade, and in opening up Canadian markets to the producers of other countries who wish to do business on a fair and reciprocal basis.
Our best customer, and the customer who also supplies us with many of the things we need, is the United States of America. We have come a long way from the "no truck or trade with the Yankees" slogan of the Conservatives in 1911. Some years ago a new trade policy was inaugurated, with the passing of the reciprocal trade agreements act. President Roosevelt sponsored a policy of lowering tariff barriers, and our Liberal government at Ottawa was quick to take advantage of the chance to negotiate a trade treaty which gave our fishermen access to the United States market. The duty against codfish, for instance, was reduced from a cent to three-quarters of a cent a pound, and later to half a cent. In 1947 came the general agreement on tariffs and trade under which we secured concessions on practically all species of fish- fresh, frozen, dried, smoked and canned- concessions which were enlarged and confirmed in subsequent revisions at the Annecy and Torquay conferences.
I know this tariff problem is not just a Canadian problem. Over a number of years our Liberal governments have been progressively reducing tariffs, sometimes by

The Budget-Mr. J. R. Kirk negotiation with other countries in return for cuts in their tariffs, sometimes on its own initiative, as in the present budget. As a result, Canada is now one of the lowest tariff countries in the world.
In my opinion the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated on the tax reductions he has announced. The radio licence fee had outlived its usefulness, and was costly to collect. Since almost everyone uses a radio nowadays, the cost of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation service can be taken out of the proceeds of taxation on radio receiving sets, with much less difficulty and with more fairness; and similarly, the cost of television will be borne by those who purchase television sets. The removal of the stamp tax on cheques, which was a nuisance, will be welcomed by Canadians generally.
As I have already observed, our friends in the opposition are hard put to criticize this budget. What can they expect? They have been saying taxes were too high. Now that taxes are reduced, they claim the rich benefit more than the poor. But I believe that all fair-minded Canadian taxpayers will agree that the time has come when those who put their capital to work for the general productivity of the country should receive some incentive to invest still more heavily in Canada's development, and thereby increase both production and employment.
Before commenting further on the recent tax reductions and their effect upon the Canadian economy, I should like to speak briefly of several matters of special interest and importance to the people of the maritime provinces, and especially to those concerned directly with the primary industries of fishing and farming.
I am particularly concerned with the everpresent risks which must be faced by those who go down to the sea in ships, to wrest their livelihood from the unyielding ocean. As hon. members may know, I have repeatedly brought to the attention of this house the great need of increased aids to navigation; and, in this connection, I must express my appreciation of the co-operation received from that branch of the Department of Transport. I realize that with shortages of important metals it has not been possible in recent years to provide new equipment as readily as might be desirable. But now that supply has caught up pretty well with demand, it is to be hoped that out of date buoys will be replaced by more modern ones and that the shoals and rocks along our coast will be still more clearly marked for the guidance of our fishermen; for they must venture forth long before the breaking day provides a light 
for their path, and return home after darkness has hidden these hazards from view.
I want to stress once again, also, the need of a coastguard service, to provide improved search and rescue facilities for ships in distress. At present there are, it is true, several agencies of government which provide some such service; but a Canadian coastguard service could combine all these into one well-trained organization which would operate more economically and more effectively, and which could serve in time of emergency as another arm of the naval service. I do hope the time is not far distant when the representations which have been made from various sources in support of such a service will produce results, and a Canadian coastguard service will become a reality.
I welcome the financial assistance which is being made available in the construction of cold storage and bait freezing plants and equipment, by both the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Agriculture. The result of this has been a considerable increase in the number of such plants being installed.
While dealing with our fishing industry, I would like to urge that some form of government-sponsored insurance scheme be considered to protect our fishermen against storm losses. On several occasions during the past two seasons alone they have suffered tremendous losses to their boats and gear, and in some cases even loss of limb or life, through sudden storms, with no way of recouping their losses. Whether this insurance protection should be through federal or provincial legislation, or a combination of both, is a matter for consideration; but it is surely time for some solution of this problem which has always harassed our fishermen.
Another matter which is, in my opinion, of paramount importance, is the possibility of including our fishermen and our farmers under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Some will say that this presents unsurmountable obstacles, but I am satisfied that in this, as in other realms, where there is a will there is a way. The unemployment insurance fund has become a bulwark of protection for many groups of our Canadian wage earners, and none are more subject to periods of unemployment than are those engaged in these primary industries.
Referring to the criticism of the opposition that there is nothing in the budget for the farmer, I may say that the answer to this claim is to be found in the able speech delivered on Thursday last in this debate by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).

It is a satisfaction to the farmers of the maritime provinces that the federal government has continued to pay a subsidy on feed grain shipments from the prairie provinces. This has been a great boon to our farmers, and all are hopeful that this particular subsidy will not only be continued, but will become a definite part of the federal government's policy, for excessive freight rates make it impossible for the farmers of the east to finance the full transportation charges.
Assistance to the dairy industry, by way of federal purchasing of surplus quantities of dried milk, and price support for that commodity, will be good news to those engaged in dairy farming. At the same time, the government of Nova Scotia has brought down legislation this year banning the manufacture and sale of imitation dairy products, except peanut butter and margarine, which will be of great benefit to our dairymen.
I hope the federal government will follow up this legislation with amendments to its pure food laws as applied to the manufacture and sale of dairy substitutes.
It was good news for Canadian farmers, too, that the United States authorities had lifted the ban on Canadian livestock entering the United States market; and in this connection I would like to add my voice to all those who have acclaimed the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his officials for the prompt and efficient way in which the disastrous foot-and-mouth disease was banished from this country.
I am in full agreement with various members from all sides of the house who have spoken in support of the removal of the means test from pensions for the blind, and from recipients of war veterans allowances. These are two groups of Canadians who through no fault of their own are greatly handicapped and should not be subject to this test, which is at the least embarrassing, and at the most unjust in many instances. I urge the minister and the government to give very serious and sympathetic consideration to the possibility of removing this means test.
I wish to compliment our new Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) upon setting up a committee to review the whole matter of rural mail services. I hope that as a result of the recommendations which the committee will present to parliament many of the inadequate rates now being paid will be eliminated. We have no group of public servants more faithful to their duties, nor any whose occupational hazards are greater or more numerous. They are subject to all
The Budget-Mr. J. R. Kirk the vagaries of wind and weather, of highway and railway conditions, and I have nothing but admiration for those who deliver Her Majesty's mails to rural post offices and rural mail boxes.
However, I would have liked to see the terms of reference extended to include rural post offices and rural postmasters. The rentals paid for the former and the salaries paid to the latter are far from commensurate with the service involved. They have no basis of comparison with present-day rents and salaries, for they are still based upon what was considered modest remuneration back in the horse and buggy era. I know that our Post Office Department is doing its best to overcome these deficiencies, but it is bound by the legislation which limits its actions.
I feel that these matters could well have been included for consideration by the present committee, and I hope they will be placed before the committee when next it is set up.
It is gratifying to note that the cabinet has under consideration the distribution again this year of federal grants to our universities. However, I hope that the basis of awarding such grants will differ from that used last year. As I understand it, the money voted by parliament last year was apportioned according to the population of each province, at 50 cents a head. Nova Scotia suffered greatly from this system, for the reason that the province has a higher proportion of its population attending university than is the case in most provinces. As a result, the aid per student in Nova Scotia was the lowest of any province. Were this federal aid allocated on a national basis, with the government establishing a national rate per student, the disparity would disappear and a more equitable basis of division be arrived at.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks have dealt principally with the primary industries of farming and fishing. These are of special interest to me inasmuch as most of my constituents in Antigonish and Guysborough counties are farmers and fishermen, and the well-being of our communities depends to a very great extent upon the success of these two industries.
In Guysborough county, particularly, where there is no rail connection, those engaged in farming, fishing and lumbering find transportation a very serious matter. You perhaps will recall, Mr. Speaker, the several occasions on which I have spoken in this house of the necessity of completing the Guysborough railway. The first occasion was on February 28, 1939, before the outbreak of world war II. Then, during the war years, I refrained from mentioning the Guysborough

The announcement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that a contract has been awarded for the construction of a lock in connection with the Canso causeway will be of particular interest to eastern Canada. However, with the completion of the causeway a new problem arises. The town of Mulgrave on the mainland, and the towns of Port Hawkesbury and Point Tupper on the Cape Breton side, which are railway towns, will suffer greatly from the loss of this means of livelihood and it is their fear that they will become ghost towns. I understand that the resources and development branch of the Canadian National Railways, and the department of industry in Nova Scotia, have been giving some thought to ways and means of attracting new industries to these towns, and I sincerely hope that something concrete will materialize as a result of their endeavours.
There is no doubt that these towns will have one of the finest harbours in the world 

when the causeway has been completed, a harbour free of ice the year round. It seems to me this will provide a particularly advantageous site for industry, with the added features of a plenteous supply of coal, steel, water and hydro power near at hand. Naturally I am particularly interested in the town of Mulgrave, which is in my constituency, on the mainland; and I cannot urge too strongly that no stone be left unturned to bring one or more industries to this area.

5.	Continuance of subsidy on feed grain shipments;
6.	Improved legislation re manufacture and sale of dairy substitutes;
7.	Removal of means test from pensions for the blind;
8.	Removal of means test from war veterans allowances;
9.	Increased rentals for rural post offices;

In all of these matters, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken with the utmost sincerity and I do not think that any of these representations can be regarded as exorbitant or extravagant.
It seems to me that the financial statement which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was able to present in his budget this year means that Canada has definitely and successfully rounded another corner. We are now able to support an expanded defence effort, maintain a sound system of social security and carry a war-inflated debt. The minister, by this series of surplus-producing budgets, and thanks to the steady expansion of the nation's economy, has put Canada in a position to defend itself and to move forward with confidence. We can now look forward to the consideration of further measures of social security, larger grants for hospital construction and health services, as

steps toward the goal of adequate health service for all Canadians, regardless of where they live or what their personal income might be.
Given a continuance of sound fiscal policy and Liberal administration, Canada will continue to grow in population and to expand national production. That will happen if Canada continues to be, as it has been in the past, a good place in which to live and work, a country of freedom not merely from personal and political restraints but from restraints on initiative in business. Then we shall truly attain the goal so ably described by our Prime Minister-"to maintain our country in unity and security, as the homeland of a free people".

One more comment and I shall resume my seat. What I shall say now is in answer to something said by the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. McWilliam). I compliment the hon. member upon having made this remark, because I realize he was fighting in the interests of his own constituency, and I approve his doing so. Indeed, ever since I came to the House of Commons I have been trying to do the same thing-fighting for the rights of my people in Gloucester county.
As I said before in the house, we have now in my county a major ore development. It now looks as though some of the veins are running into Northumberland county, and we are pleased to know that. However, tonight the hon. member for Northumberland suggested that the mineral should be transported by spur line to the Miramichi, a famous river in his constituency, and exported from that point because, as he said- and I shall try to use his words-there is no deep-water terminal available at Bathurst.

Well, according to the best available information, a large smelter is going to be built at or near the town of Bathurst-because, after all, the ore body cannot be moved into Northumberland; it will remain in Gloucester. As I say, the smelter will be built at or near Bathurst, and we are certainly insisting that the export of that mineral shall be carried out from Bathurst and neighbouring ports in Gloucester county. Provided the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) shows any generosity toward us, Bathurst harbour can be made one of the best harbours on the north shore. As I said in my earlier speech, we have deep-sea harbours such as Pointe Marcel and Shippigan in my county, with which any of the harbours on the Miramichi mentioned by my hon. friend cannot compare.
So we have everything in Gloucester. We have the ore body; we will have the smelter and, with the co-operation of this government, we will have the harbour. So through the generosity of the Minister of Public Works the ore can be exported from the county of Gloucester, through the port of Bathurst, and other ports as well, as soon as our ports are made available.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate
myself with what has been said by other members on this side of the house in complimenting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Those of us who are supporters of the government can certainly take some pride in the fact that we are associated in our endeavours to maintain responsible government in Canada, and that the Canadian people have faith in this government as an administration worthy of their endorsation.
In the debate on the budget the opposition members have used two directly contradictory criticisms over and over again. They have said, first of all, that it was an election budget, and, secondly, that it was a rich man's budget. I just cannot see how they can have it both ways. If they say it is an election budget, if the minister is attempting to bribe the people with their own money, then how can it be a rich man's budget, or vice versa? I still think it is a good one. In fact the more I study its terms the more I am convinced that it is one of the very best budgets that could have been brought down under the present circumstances.
The opposition have always levelled some criticism at the fact that in the year 1949, which was an election year, there were certain reductions in taxes. They then glibly state that a year or so later these taxes were restored and they imply that perhaps after the next election the present reductions will be removed and the taxes will be increased.
The Budget-Mr. Simmons This simply is not a fair criticism, because all the people of Canada know that it was necessary to increase taxes in 1950 on the outbreak of trouble in Korea. We all know that the price of freedom is high, and no matter what the cost it is well worth it. It is gratifying to note that, although we are still at war in Korea or engaged in police action there, our congenial Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), by good administration, has been able to reduce the tax level, particularly the income tax level, to what it was in pre-Korea days.
Again let me reiterate that the people of Canada should be proud-and I believe they are-that we have such an able minister to handle our budget affairs. It may be of interest to note that to date I have not received one word of criticism from any constituents with respect to the new budget, and I believe this applies throughout the length and breadth of Canada. The only comment I have received from the north is in praise of the budget. I should like to quote an excerpt from a letter I received this morning from Mr. James F. MacDonald, one of the highly respected old-timers of the Yukon Territory. He says in part:
I am proud that we have the most progressive, honest government in Canada, and I think the best the world has ever known.
That is what our old-timers in the north think of the government and I do not believe they are very far wrong.
I believe that in a very few years the development of our Canadian northwest will be a factor to be considered in the preparation of the budget of the government of this country. This section of Canada, often referred to in bygone days as the frozen north, is without doubt on the threshold of what will be one of the most beneficial and far-reaching developments Canada has yet experienced. I do not refer only to quartz or placer mining or to the development of its timber, agricultural or fishery products. Our great expansion in the northwest is coming in the field of hydroelectric power, with that power actually used in the north for industrial purposes.
More and more electric power is daily being used in developing our natural products, and cheap power in great amounts has become the key to the economics of the recovery and processing of products like aluminum, chromium, iron, nickel and crude oil. There are still many great power sites yet unexploited in Canada, and some of the greatest among these are to be found in Labrador, British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. This power is now being considered for development and use in what can be called a metallurgical

Where available in great quantities it makes possible electric smelting and the manufacture of invaluable alloys using iron, silver, copper, chromium, titanium, tungsten and other base metals that will give metal fabrics and shapes of unheard-of strength, toughness and durability, combined with amazing lightness.
One of the great potential power sites in Canada is in the great Yukon river drainage basin in my constituency of the Yukon Territory and in northwestern British Columbia. Here a high interior plateau with great quantities of water and the Atlin lake and the Yukon river system make feasible tremendous power developments. Ventures Limited, through its associated companies, Frobisher Limited and Quebec Metallurgical Industries, is considering at this moment one of Canada's largest power projects in this area, that will involve eventually the production of from 4 to 5 million horsepower.
It has several great features: First, the water used will be from the great Yukon river drainage basin, including the Yukon and Teslin rivers in the Yukon Territory, the reaches of the Alsek river and its tributaries and water from the Kluane river watershed northwest of Whitehorse. Second, power will be developed in plants in Canada and will be used in large metallurgical processing plants built and operated in Canada. Ores from the Yukon and northern British Columbia areas will be treated, as well as large quantities of ores brought in from different parts of the world. Large quantities of low-priced power and new smelting and metallurgical processes will bring an industrial age to our Canadian northwest. Field surveys by air and ground are being planned and water flow readings expanded with the objective of a rapid and orderly development of one of the northwest's greatest resources, hydroelectric power.
I am naturally delighted that our north Pacific area, and particularly the Yukon and Northwest Territories where the federal government has administrative responsibilities, seems to be coming into its own, and also that this future development will be under the auspices of private enterprise with every attention paid to furthering Canadian interests. I hope that those responsible for the administration of our northern areas will give the fullest co-operation to those actively engaged in the development. I am sure that all relative information in federal government and provincial departments will be readily available.
At this point I wish to mention a need that no doubt the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) already realizes,


the necessity of increased hydrometric survey work in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Fortunately, in 1950 the measurement of stream flow in these areas was expanded but present studies are still being hindered by lack of flow data. This is particularly the case in regard to winter flow readings of streams, which is so important in northern latitudes. I would also like to suggest that whenever level lines are run in any Canadian area by federal or in fact provincial parties, a special effort be made to secure water level readings on the main streams and lakes that may be conveniently near or adjacent to the surveys being made. I understand that the geodetic service of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is now making a special effort to collect this information which always seems to be necessary before we expect it will be required.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just think of what the future holds in new wealth when this potential water power is harnessed and put to work to develop the vast mineral wealth of northwestern Canada. Mining is the dominant industry in these northern areas and is bound to play an ever-increasing part in the economic life of the northland and of Canada, as the vast mineral treasures now hidden are developed, processed and made available to supply the demands of Canada and the other free nations of the world. And this proposed development of hydroelectric power is bound to have a vital effect on the mining industry and on the lives and interests of the people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories for the benefit of this and future generations.
Mr. Speaker, I might digress here and say that the development of the territories is fast reaching the point where local selfgovernment is within the foreseeable future. Hon. members would be the first to agree that no people can be satisfied unless they have complete self-government. No matter how considerate the departmental administration is, resource administration approximately
4,000	miles away cannot be entirely satisfactory. We can now look to the day, and not too distant, when both the Yukon and the Northwest Territories will have their own wholly elected legislatures with all the rights of a province. One of the first considerations should be the transfer of the local administration or resources administration with its many aspects and problems. The very strength of confederation lies in the fact that selfgovernment is enjoyed by the several provinces, though not of course by the territories. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it would be in the best Canadian tradition to resort to local self-government as soon as we have sufficient

population and industry. The majority of the people of the territories definitely are supporters of this view.
I would like to tell hon. members something about the known mineral resources of this vast northland which covers about two-fifths of the area of Canada. The gold placer deposits of the Yukon are well known and the story has been told in song and legend for many years. Up to the end of 1951 the total value of gold produced had almost reached the one-third of a billion dollar mark. In the Mayo-Keno district of the Yukon is a highly mineralized area producing silver, lead, zinc, cadmium and gold. Although the area has not been tested in depth it has the second largest silver mine in Canada, and is believed to be the fourth largest silver producer in the world. In 1952 this one mine alone, as quoted in the Northern Miner of January 29,	1953, produced 1,353,304
ounces of silver, 5,169,235 pounds of lead and 3,284,644 pounds of zinc. In addition there are numerous properties coming into production in this area.
In the Whitehorse district there is a known copper belt extending for about 300 miles from Whitehorse to Alaska. This area was high-graded in the early part of the century around Whitehorse and, incidentally, produced the famous Kennecott copper mine in Alaska. Last summer there was a very rich find of nickel-copper ore near the Alaska highway about 200 miles west of Whitehorse on Quill creek, which, if early promise is fulfilled, should rival the Sudbury area in wealth and production.
In other areas scattered throughout the Yukon there are known to be rich deposits of antimony, tungsten, molybdenum, asbestos, quartz, gold, silver, lead, zinc, copper and iron. With the potential of several million horsepower of electrical energy awaiting development in the Yukon Territory and adjoining parts of northern British Columbia, think of what the future holds in store for the northern part of this great dominion.
In the Northwest Territories we have the uranium production at Eldorado on Great Bear lake; the great gold deposits in the Yellowknife district; the lead-zinc deposits at Pine Point on the south side of Great Slave lake, at O'Connor lake and at the east end of Great Slave lake; the vast nickel deposits in the Keewatin district; copper deposits along the Arctic rim; and a variety of precious and strategic minerals in an area stretching from the east end of Great Slave lake to Chesterfield inlet on Hudson bay.
In addition to this there is a vast area extending from the northern boundaries of British Columbia and Alberta and along the
The Budget-Mr. Simmons Mackenzie river valley to the Arctic coast, which is favourable for deposits of oil and gas. I have been told that approximately 35,000,000 acres have been staked for exploratory oil and gas permits. This gives you some idea of the importance to Canada of the mining industry in the north.
I would like to say a word here, Mr. Speaker, about the role played by the prospectors. Almost every mine of any consequence today owes its discovery to the individual prospector. These hardy, resourceful pioneers are the lifeblood of the mining industry, and the government should do everything possible to afford them encouragement and assistance, both financial and otherwise. Anyone who has been in mountainous country need not be told that those who prospect the area must have a good constitution. They must be able to travel long distances on foot and to endure many hardships on meagre rations. Before them always is the lure of the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Their returns are generally small, but their efforts have provided the mining claims which go to make up the producing mines we have today. Without their initiative and fortitude, combined with the pioneering spirit, there would be very few producing mines in Canada today.
As I have said before, development of the waterpower and mineral resources in the Yukon and Northwest Territories will be considerably accelerated in the near future and is going to play an increasingly important role in the industrial and economic life of the nation. Therefore I hope every encouragement and assistance will be given by this government, and I have every confidence that this government, and particularly the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), will bring this about.
One of the important requirements for the development of these northern areas is improved transportation facilities. We all know what the construction of the Alaska highway, the Whitehorse-Mayo road and the Atlin road have meant to the recent development of the Yukon Territory and northern British Columbia, and what the construction of the Mackenzie highway has meant to the Northwest Territories. If the development of the mineral wealth of these areas which I have mentioned is to be brought about it will require more and more transportation facilities.
The Alaska highway has completed its tenth year of operation. It has been a key to the opening up of northern British Columbia, the Yukon and Alaska. Much of the industrial development you hear of, such as the Cassiar asbestos mine on McDame creek,

The Budget-Mr. Simmons was made possible as a result of the Alaska highway. The Hudson Bay Mining Company, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and many other companies have been able to speed up their prospecting work through being able to get in quickly to points on the highway near these favourable mineral areas. The same situation applied in connection with the Mackenzie highway from Grimshaw, Alberta to Hay River in the Northwest Territories.
The Alaska highway has become one of the great tourist attractions of the world, and more and more people are planning a summer vacation along that romantic road through the northland. It was built by the United States government in co-operation with the government of Canada, and will stand for all time as a memorial to Franklin D. Roosevelt and Mackenzie King, the two great statesmen who planned it. I have travelled the length of the Alaska highway on several occasions, and each year sees the development of new communities throughout its entire length. We now have modern facilities at the various stopping places. The best of food is served and modern facilities are provided by those courteous people who cater to the strangers who travel the highway.
The highway is being well maintained, and here I must pay a tribute to the Canadian army for continuing to maintain and improve this great public thoroughfare. Army units are established throughout its length and the most modern of roadbuilding equipment is in operation. It seems to me that this is an ideal way to maintain a great arterial highway so important to our national economy and defence.
You will recall that in the early days the royal engineers came out from England to build the great Cariboo highway in British Columbia. They made such a fine job of it that for many miles it continues today, as they left it. In placing the military in charge of the Alaska highway the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is following an ancient tradition so far as the Pacific coast is concerned. It is to the credit of the army that the heaviest traffic is able to use the highway every hour of every day of the year.
Not only has the Alaska highway been a key instrument in the development of solid materials; it has been of tremendous assistance in the search for oil in northern British Columbia and the Yukon. The Alaska highway offers a safe and swift thoroughfare over which the drilling crews and the geophysical prospectors may proceed. I might say that recent showings indicate prospects of oil and natural gas along that portion of the highway 

from Dawson Creek, British Columbia to Watson Lake in the Yukon Territory. The same conditions apply along the Mackenzie highway from northern Alberta to the Northwest Territories.
If the backlog of wealth which we have in the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories and in northern British Columbia is to be developed for the benefit of Canada and the world, more attention must be paid to providing even more efficient methods of transportation. I think it is about time that favourable consideration was given by the department concerned to the hard surfacing of the Canadian portion of the Alaska highway. Hard surfacing of this highway would reduce the cost of maintenance considerably and would make for greater safety by eliminating the dust hazard, thereby contributing to the better health of the armed services personnel and the public generally. Quantities of asphalt can be obtained in the western provinces, which makes it possible to secure cheap supplies.
While the highway has served and is serving a great need, and while the air lines are steadily helping to open up the country, the major transportation need of the north is that of rail communication. We need a railroad from the heart of America to Alaska. It could very well be an extension of the Canadian National Railways from Prince George, British Columbia, through the great Rocky mountains trench, where a water grade exists, clear through to Whitehorse and on to Fairbanks, Alaska. Military men are well informed of the importance of such a service, and the industrial people will never be able to develop maximum production in that area until a railroad is constructed.
Discovery of oil in the Peace river country greatly simplifies the problem of providing rail transportation north. In the old days it would have been necessary to provide coal for the locomotives over that long haul. Today the diesel engine would use diesel fuel produced north and west of Edmonton, and the cost of operating the railroad would be greatly reduced below the mark estimated by the United States army which seriously considered railroad construction from Prince George through Whitehorse to Fairbanks, Alaska, during the last war.
Absence of a railroad of course provides more and more business for the trucking concerns. I must pay my tribute to those sturdy operators of truck lines throughout the north who brave all weather conditions in order to bring to the civilian population and to the military outposts merchandise of all kinds, without which we would find it a hardship to exist in the north.
